summary: Extends Mobile IP so a device with several network interfaces, such as Wi-Fi and cellular, can register an address for each and keep multiple tunnels to its home agent at once. This allows the device to use all its interfaces together. It is an experimental specification.

eli5.summary: A phone with Wi-Fi and cellular is like a person with two doors to the house. This lets it use both doors at the same time.

questions: how can a mobile node use multiple interfaces with mobile ip
what is flow binding in mobile ip
how can a mobile device use multiple network interfaces with mobile ip
subtitle: Multi-interface mobile devices can use all their network connections at once.

tldr.problem: Mobile devices like smartphones have Wi-Fi, cellular, and other interfaces but Mobile IP only lets them use one at a time for their home address traffic, wasting bandwidth.
tldr.mechanism: The device registers a care-of address for each interface with its home agent and establishes multiple tunnels simultaneously. The device and home agent can negotiate which flows use which tunnel.
tldr.outcome: Mobile devices can bond multiple interfaces for higher bandwidth and intelligent routing, with control over which applications use which network.

today: RFC 7629 is an experimental RFC and has not been adopted as a standard. It remains an optional extension that home agents and mobile nodes can implement to enable multi-interface aggregation, but it is not yet a required capability of Mobile IP.

sections.title: Introduction and the Multi-Interface Problem
sections.content:
Modern mobile devices are equipped with multiple wireless interfaces: Wi-Fi, LTE, CDMA, and others. However, Mobile IP (RFC 5944) creates only a single tunnel from the mobile node to its home agent. All traffic using the mobile node's home address must flow through that one tunnel, even if the device is connected to multiple networks. This means only one interface can be actively used for home-address traffic at a time, wasting the potential bandwidth of unused interfaces.

This specification extends Mobile IP to allow a mobile node with multiple interfaces to register each interface separately with its home agent and to maintain multiple concurrent tunnels. The mobile node can then leverage all available network interfaces simultaneously, achieving higher aggregated bandwidth. Additionally, the mobile node and home agent can negotiate flow policies that bind specific IP traffic flows to specific tunnels based on criteria like the source port or protocol type.
sections.eli5: Mobile devices have multiple ways to connect: Wi-Fi and cellular. Before, the phone could only use one for its home network traffic. Now it can use both at the same time.

sections.title: Multipath and Binding Concepts
sections.content:
The specification introduces two new message extensions to Mobile IP. The Multipath extension (Section 4.1) allows a mobile node to indicate in its Registration Request that it wants to register an additional care-of address (the IP address it is using on a particular interface) while keeping previous registrations active. Without this, each new registration would replace the previous one.

Each registration is assigned a unique Binding Identifier (BID). A binding is the association between the mobile node's home address and one of its care-of addresses. Multiple bindings with different BIDs allow the mobile node to have multiple active tunnels to its home agent, one for each registered interface.

Figure 1 of the RFC shows a mobile node connected to WLAN, LTE, and CDMA networks, each with its own care-of address (CoA_1, CoA_2, CoA_3) and tunnel (Tunnel_1, Tunnel_2, Tunnel_3). The home agent manages all three bindings and can route traffic according to negotiated policies.
sections.eli5: Each connection (Wi-Fi, cellular, etc.) gets its own tunnel to the home network. The home agent remembers all of them and can send traffic down any tunnel.

sections.title: Message Extensions
sections.content:
The Multipath extension is a non-skippable extension added to Mobile IP Registration Requests. It indicates that the sender is requesting to register the care-of address in the request as one of many care-of addresses, rather than replacing the previous one. The extension also carries information specific to the interface to which the care-of address is bound.

The Flow-Binding extension (Section 4.2) allows a mobile node to propose or acknowledge traffic flow policies. A flow policy specifies which flows should use which care-of address, with a preference order and fallback behavior. For example: SIP traffic prefers Tunnel_1 (Wi-Fi), falls back to Tunnel_2 (LTE) if Wi-Fi is unavailable, and is dropped if neither is available.

The extension includes Flow Identifiers (FIDs) that match flows based on source address, destination address, protocol type, source port, destination port, and other parameters as defined in RFC 6088.
sections.eli5: The mobile node tells the home agent: "I have Wi-Fi and cellular connected, please send SIP calls over Wi-Fi first, and video over cellular."

sections.title: Protocol Operation and Negotiation
sections.content:
When a mobile node attaches to a new interface and obtains a new care-of address, it sends a Registration Request with the Multipath extension. The home agent, upon accepting the request, responds with a Registration Reply code of 0 (success) and establishes a new tunnel between itself and the mobile node using the new care-of address.

If the mobile node includes the Flow-Binding extension, the home agent examines the proposed flow policy and may modify or acknowledge it. Both the home agent and mobile node are then responsible for enforcing the negotiated policy: the home agent routes flows according to the policy when sending traffic to the mobile node through the appropriate tunnel, and the mobile node sends its flows through the appropriate tunnel to the home agent.

The call flow in Section 3.1 of the RFC illustrates a mobile node attaching to WLAN (steps 1-4) and then to LTE (steps 5-8), with the home agent accepting both registrations and establishing both tunnels. Subsequent traffic is then routed according to the negotiated flow policy.
sections.eli5: When the phone connects to a new network, it tells the home agent and they both set up a tunnel. If the phone sends a flow policy, both sides agree on which tunnel each type of traffic should use.

sections.title: Routing and Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Multiple concurrent tunnels to the home agent create an overlay routing topology. Each tunnel represents a separate logical path, and the mobile node can distribute its traffic across them. The routing behavior depends on how the flow policy is configured and whether it includes preferences and fallback mechanisms.

The specification is particularly useful for scenarios where different networks have different characteristics. For example, a mobile node might prefer LTE for voice (low-latency), Wi-Fi for downloads (high-bandwidth), and keep CDMA as a backup. The home agent has the capability to apply these policies consistently to traffic flowing in both directions.

The specification defines new error codes for Registration Reply messages to handle cases where the home agent cannot support multipath or flow binding. Mobile nodes must be prepared to operate without these extensions if the home agent does not support them.
sections.eli5: The device can choose which tunnel to use for each type of traffic. Voice calls go over low-latency LTE, big downloads over fast Wi-Fi, and everything has a backup if one network fails.

layers.label: Home Agent
layers.detail: Manages all tunnels and applies policies
